shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Germany's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Seventy-six percent. {p} That's how rich the average Pole is, compared with the average German, this year: income per person, adjusted for prices. About sixty thousand dollars against seventy-nine thousand. {pp} In 1990, it was thirty percent. Poland crossed forty percent of Germany's level in 2004, the year it joined the European Union. Half in 2012. Sixty percent in 2020. Seventy in 2024. {p} The IMF has it at eighty-three percent by 2031. So there's one question left, and it's the dotted line at the top: when does Poland reach a hundred?

On this channel, Poland has been passing countries all year. Japan, this year. Spain, next year, in the IMF's forecast. Italy, right after 2031. {p} Germany is a different kind of race. Japan and Italy were barely moving. Germany is the biggest economy in Europe, and it's also Poland's biggest customer: more than a quarter of everything Poland sells abroad goes to Germany. So Poland is trying to catch the economy it depends on. {pp} <soft>Here's how the gap closed, why the last few years were the fastest yet, and the two dates the numbers point to.</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this is a series, and the next episode is Poland versus Czechia, the one neighbor Poland still hasn't caught. Subscribe so you don't miss it. {p} Now, the gap.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Germany's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Look at how long each step took. {p} From thirty percent of Germany to forty: fourteen years. Forty to fifty: eight. Fifty to sixty: eight again. And sixty to seventy: four. Just four years, from 2020 to 2024. {pp} In thirty-six years, Poland lost ground on Germany in only three: 1991, the first year of shock therapy, and then by less than half a point in 2001 and 2010. Every other year, this line went up. {p} So why did it speed up after 2019? Not only because Poland ran faster. Because Germany stopped.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Germany (annual %); 2026 is an IMF estimate
shots.narration: Here's Germany's growth, year by year, after inflation. {p} 2020, the pandemic: minus four percent. A rebound in 2021. Then 2023: minus one. 2024: zero. 2025: zero point two. {pp} Add it up, and Germany's economy in 2025 was less than one percent bigger than in 2019. Six years, almost no growth. Poland's grew about eighteen percent over the same six years. {p} The IMF expects Germany to pick up a little this year, to about one point three percent, then slow again, to zero point six by 2031.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH), population (LP)
shots.title: Why Germany stalled
shots.narration: Three things hit Germany at once. {p} Energy: until 2022, Russia supplied more than half of Germany's gas imports. Then the war cut that off, and German factories suddenly paid far more for energy. {p} Cars: the industry at the heart of the German economy is losing ground in China, its biggest market, to Chinese brands. {p} And people: Germany's population peaked in 2024 at about eighty-three and a half million, and the IMF has it falling from here. {pp} None of that makes Germany poor. It makes it slow. Since 2001, Germany's economy has grown about one percent a year. Poland's: about three and a half.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · unemployment rate (% of labor force), 2026 estimate
shots.title: Unemployment, 2026
shots.narration: And on some measures, Poland has already arrived. {p} Unemployment this year: about three point two percent in Poland, {pp} four percent in Germany. Poland's rate has been lower than Germany's every year since 2020. In 2004, Poland's was nineteen percent, almost twice Germany's.

shots.src: Eurostat · regional GDP per inhabitant in PPS, % of EU average, 2024 (NUTS 2)
shots.title: Output per person, % of EU average, 2024
shots.narration: Then there's Warsaw. {p} By the EU statistics office's numbers for 2024, the Warsaw region produces about a hundred and fifty-seven percent of the EU average per person, adjusted for prices. Berlin: a hundred and twenty-seven. Warsaw is also ahead of every region of the former East Germany, all of them below the EU average. {pp} Capitals flatter these numbers, because commuters are counted where they work, and Munich's region and Hamburg are still well ahead of Warsaw. But a Polish city out-producing Berlin would have sounded absurd in 1990.

stats.label: best region of former East Germany (Leipzig)

shots.narration: Now, the catch. Two of them, actually. {p} And if you're enjoying this, the subscribe button is right there. The series continues with Czechia.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ (NGDPDPC), and PPP gap in US$ (PPPPC)
shots.title: Per person: plain dollars, and the dollar gap
shots.narration: First: everything so far was adjusted for prices. In plain dollars, the average German produces about sixty-six thousand this year, and the average Pole about thirty-one thousand. Less than half. In 1990, it was eight percent. By 2031, the IMF has it at about fifty-five. {pp} Second: percentages can hide dollars. Even in price-adjusted terms, the gap in dollars kept growing for almost thirty years: from about fifteen thousand in 1990 to almost twenty-five thousand in 2018. A slow one percent on Germany's big number added more dollars than a fast four percent on Poland's small one. {p} The dollar gap has only been shrinking since 2019: about eighteen thousand six hundred this year, and about fifteen thousand eight hundred by 2031.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · general government gross debt (% of GDP), 2026 estimate; IMF series start in 1995
shots.title: Government debt, % of GDP, 2026
shots.narration: And there's one thing Poland does pass Germany on this year, and it's not the good kind. Government debt: about sixty-seven percent of the economy, {pp} against Germany's sixty-five. The first time Poland's ratio is above Germany's in IMF data going back to 1995. Part of it is defense: Poland now spends more on its military, as a share of its economy, than any other NATO member.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · PPPPC; parity years are Chartbound extrapolations of the 2016–2026 and IMF 2026–2031 paces, not IMF forecasts
shots.title: When does Poland reach 100%?
shots.narration: So, when does the line hit a hundred? {p} The IMF's forecast stops in 2031, at eighty-three percent. Beyond that, there's no official number, so here are two honest ones. {p} If the next ten years look like the last ten, when Poland closed in on Germany by more than three percent a year, Poland reaches Germany's level around 2034. {p} If the IMF's slower pace holds beyond 2031, with Poland growing two and a half percent a year and Germany under one, it's around 2043. {pp} Nine years apart. And the difference comes down to two things: whether Germany grows again, and whether Poland keeps growing while its own population shrinks. About thirty-six million people today, down from almost thirty-nine million at its peak in 1999.

And here's the strange part about this race. Poland's growth was built on German factories, German customers and German supply chains. A Germany that stops growing makes Poland's line on this chart rise faster, and makes life harder for the Polish companies that sell to it. {p} The best outcome for Poland isn't Germany falling. It's both lines going up, with Poland's going up faster. That's what happened from 2004 to 2019, and it took Poland from forty percent of Germany to almost sixty.

<soft>So, your guess: 2034, 2043, or never?</soft> Tell me in the comments. {p} If you're watching from Germany: does the slowdown feel real where you live? {p} And if you're watching from Poland: which country should I cover after Czechia? I read every comment.
Italy is the next big country on Poland's list, and by 2031 the gap is four hundred and ninety-nine dollars. That story is right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Poland Is 76% of Germany. When Does It Catch Up?
yt.description:
Income per person, adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): Poland was 30% of Germany in 1990, 40% in 2004, 50% in 2012, 60% in 2020, 70% in 2024 and is 76% this year; the IMF has 83% in 2031. Why the last steps were the fastest (Germany's economy barely grew from 2019 to 2025), where Poland is already ahead (unemployment; Warsaw vs Berlin), the two catches (plain dollars and the dollar gap), and two dates for parity: ~2034 at the 2016–2026 pace, ~2043 at the IMF's pace.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP, LUR, GGXWDG_NGDP); Eurostat regional GDP per inhabitant in PPS, 2024; NATO defence expenditure estimates (2025). Parity years are extrapolations, not IMF forecasts.
{music_credits}
